hypothesis.title: Cache stampede (thundering herd) on popular SKUs
hypothesis.explanation: The 2-second cache TTL (_cache in pricing.py) combined with 260 concurrent users hammering 5 popular SKUs causes periodic stampedes: when a cache entry expires, dozens of requests for that SKU all miss the cache and execute _compute simultaneously. This saturates DB CPU (300% observed) and inflates p99 to ~1800 ms while p50 stays at ~1 ms (cache hits). The bimodal latency (fast hits, slow misses) and high DB CPU during spikes match this pattern.
supporting_evidence: DB CPU 263–304% (3+ cores busy) while app CPU 48–59%
Only 5 SKUs are bestsellers with 120k order lines each; 260 users / 150 ms think time → high request rate per hot SKU
Cache check-then-set is not atomic across await _compute()
missing_evidence: Direct measurement of cache miss rate and compute concurrency

proposed_experiment.rationale: Measure in-process spans at baseline concurrency to quantify cache miss frequency and compute/query latency distribution.

predictions.if_supported: Count >> 150/min (expected 1 miss per 2 s per hot SKU × 5 SKUs × 30 = 750/min baseline; stampede drives it far higher)
predictions.if_refuted: Count ≈ 150–750/min (no stampede; misses match TTL rate)

hypothesis.title: Connection pool exhaustion (max_size=20 too small for 260 users)
hypothesis.explanation: The pool max_size=20 (db.py) is far below the 260 concurrent users. When demand queries run long (whether from stampede or inherent cost), connections are held, forcing new requests to queue in pool.acquire(). The db.pool_acquire span would show high p99, and db_activity would show active connections pinned at the max with wait events.
supporting_evidence: DB CPU 300% suggests many active queries
db.pool_acquire span exists in both pricing.py and orders.py
contradicting_evidence: If pool were exhausted, p50 would also rise (all requests wait), but p50 is 1 ms
missing_evidence: Active connection count vs pool max

proposed_experiment.rationale: Directly measure pool acquire latency and DB connection saturation at baseline load.

predictions.if_supported: Significant time in wait events while connections active

hypothesis.title: Demand query index contention with order-line inserts
hypothesis.explanation: POST /orders inserts into order_lines (sku, ordered_at) using the same composite index (order_lines_sku_time_idx) that the demand query scans for the last 7 days. At 83 orders/s, heavy insert volume on hot SKUs causes buffer-pin or lock contention on index pages, sporadically stalling the demand query's index scan. This would show as high db.demand_query p99 with specific PostgreSQL wait events, without requiring a cache stampede.

Demand query scans that index for last 7 days (120k rows/SKU)
DB CPU 300% could reflect buffer contention

p50 of demand query would also rise if contention were constant

db.demand_query latency at low concurrency (no insert contention)

events.message: Root cause: Cache stampede (thundering herd) on popular SKUs

single-flight-coalescing: Request coalescing (single-flight) using per-SKU asyncio.Lock. When a cache entry expires, the first request acquires the lock and computes; concurrent requests for the same SKU wait on the lock, then read the freshly populated cache entry. This eliminates the thundering-herd stampede by serializing cache misses per key.

candidate.name: single-flight-coalescing
candidate.strategy: Request coalescing (single-flight) using per-SKU asyncio.Lock. When a cache entry expires, the first request acquires the lock and computes; concurrent requests for the same SKU wait on the lock, then read the freshly populated cache entry. This eliminates the thundering-herd stampede by serializing cache misses per key.
candidate.expected_effect: Eliminates the bimodal latency tail. Cache misses no longer race for DB connections; pricing.compute p99 drops from ~2,500 ms to near the single-query latency (~500 ms). HTTP GET p99 falls well under 100 ms because the cache-hit path (p50 ~0.2 ms) dominates and misses are serialized, not amplified. DB CPU contention disappears because concurrent misses per SKU collapse to 1.
candidate.risks: Lock contention could become a new bottleneck if a single SKU is hammered by hundreds of requests for a popular SKU while its lock is held, but the critical section is only the DB query (~500 ms p99) so queueing delay is bounded. Memory leak from unbounded _locks dict is negligible (only 24 SKUs). Correctness risk: double-checked locking must re-validate cache after acquiring the lock to avoid recomputing a value another request just stored.

events.message: background-refresh-worker: Proactive background refresh worker. A dedicated asyncio task wakes every 1.5 s (shorter than the 2 s TTL) and refreshes all SKUs currently in the cache in parallel, limited by a semaphore to avoid overwhelming the connection pool. This keeps popular SKUs perpetually warm so cache misses become rare, removing the stampede trigger. The worker is started/stopped via the FastAPI lifespan so it shares the application's pool.

candidate.strategy: Proactive background refresh worker. A dedicated asyncio task wakes every 1.5 s (shorter than the 2 s TTL) and refreshes all SKUs currently in the cache in parallel, limited by a semaphore to avoid overwhelming the connection pool. This keeps popular SKUs perpetually warm so cache misses become rare, removing the stampede trigger. The worker is started/stopped via the FastAPI lifespan so it shares the application's pool.
candidate.expected_effect: Cache misses drop from ~4,700/min to near zero for hot SKUs because the background task refreshes them before TTL expiry. The thundering herd never forms. HTTP GET p99 collapses to the cache-hit path (<1 ms). DB CPU falls from 300% to baseline because demand_query calls become periodic and controlled (24 SKUs × 1 refresh/1.5 s = 16 qps, well within pool capacity). The 3-second freshness SLO is met because refresh interval (1.5 s) < TTL (2 s) < SLO (3 s).
candidate.risks: Background refresh adds constant DB load (~16 qps) even during quiet periods, but this is far below the observed stampede rate (79 qps) and pool capacity. If the pool is exhausted by foreground traffic, background refreshes may wait on pool_acquire, but the semaphore (max 10 concurrent) bounds this. Correctness risk: a SKU not yet in the cache (cold start) will still miss and compute synchronously; this is rare and self-correcting once cached. The worker must be cleanly stopped on shutdown to avoid task leaks.

events.message: stale-while-revalidate: Stale-while-revalidate (grace period) with coalesced hard misses. Each cache entry carries two timestamps: fresh_until (2 s) and expires_at (3 s, matching the SLO). Requests within fresh_until are served instantly. Requests in the grace window (fresh_until..expires_at) are served the stale value while a single background refresh is triggered (coalesced per SKU). Only after expires_at does a request synchronously compute, again coalesced via a per-SKU lock. This decouples request latency from DB latency for the vast majority of traffic.

candidate.strategy: Stale-while-revalidate (grace period) with coalesced hard misses. Each cache entry carries two timestamps: fresh_until (2 s) and expires_at (3 s, matching the SLO). Requests within fresh_until are served instantly. Requests in the grace window (fresh_until..expires_at) are served the stale value while a single background refresh is triggered (coalesced per SKU). candidate.expected_effect: HTTP GET p99 collapses to the cache-hit path (<1 ms) because 100% of requests during the 2–3 s grace window return immediately with stale data. Hard misses (after 3 s) are rare and serialized by the lock, so their tail (~500 ms) does not amplify. The 3-second freshness SLO is met by construction (expires_at = now + 3 s). DB CPU drops because background refreshes are rate-limited (one per SKU per grace window) and replace the stampede.
candidate.risks: Stale data is served for up to 1 s (the grace window), which is allowed by the 3 s SLO but means prices may lag demand by up to 3 s instead of 2 s. Background refresh errors are swallowed; a failed refresh leaves the entry stale until the next grace window or a hard miss. The _refresh_tasks dict could leak if tasks crash without cleanup, but the finally block removes them. Lock contention on hard misses is bounded because they are rare (only after 3 s of no requests).
